beats.narration_text: Hi, I'm Om Mali. Week four of the Private AI Valuation Agent. Seven companies, filing under a hundred and twenty-eight different names. This week I built the thing that decides which company a filing is actually talking about. And, more importantly, a way to prove whether it works.

The ask types itself into the composer, character by character.

Three output lines land in sequence — the ask arrives ANSWERED (COLD OPEN LAW).

beats.narration_text: Every filing writes a company's name however it likes. And if you cannot tell which company a row refers to, you cannot price anything. So this week has two halves. A matcher that decides. And a labelled set of right answers to check it against. The second half is the one that matters.

shot.visual_intent: The BLUF as kinetic type — why entity resolution gates everything, and which of the two halves is the real deliverable. No data exhibit (EXECUTIVE-SUMMARY LAW).

Two cards land side by side — 'A MATCHER that decides' and 'A LABELLED SET of right answers'.
The second card takes the terracotta border; the first dims. The verdict line sets beneath.

beats.narration_text: Databricks shows up under fifty-one different spellings. Space Exploration, twenty-eight. Anthropic, ten. Seven companies wearing a hundred and twenty-eight names between them. Those are real strings, exactly as funds typed them. And they are hiding inside three point two million distinct issuer names.

A total chip resolves to 128 beside the bars.
A column of REAL Databricks spellings scrolls up beside the chart — the repetition is the point.
The haystack counter races to 3,204,853 across the footer.

beats.narration_text: So I built a ground truth set. Three hundred and twenty-two of these strings, each labelled with the company it actually means, covering seven thousand two hundred and seventy-six holdings. Then I scored two systems against the same labels. The simple name patterns I started with, and a new deterministic matcher.

shot.visual_intent: The golden set as an object: two counters, then the same set forking into TWO systems so it is obvious both are judged against identical labels.

show.event: A labelled-set card assembles in the centre — GOLDEN SET v1.0.0.
Counter one races to 322 labelled issuer names.

show.at: on 'two systems against the same labels'
show.event: Two arrows fork out of the ONE set into two named boxes — the patterns, and the matcher.
Caption sets: the same labels judge both.

props.title: A labelled set of right answers
props.caption: The same labels judge both — which is the only reason the comparison means anything.

beats.narration_text: The patterns I started with: ninety-eight percent recall. The new matcher: a hundred percent. But precision barely moves, and I want to be exact about that. On the hardest cases the old patterns were actually cleaner. So the honest claim here is recall. Not precision.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w4-scoreboard.png (upper half). The recall column moves and the precision column deliberately does not — the beat's claim is the asymmetry, so the visual has to show precision NOT winning.

show.event: Two-row table draws with PRECISION and RECALL columns.
Row one fills: 0.9916 / 0.9792, in ink.
Row two fills: 0.9959 / 1.0000, recall cell terracotta — the only number that really moved.
A bracket marks the precision column and labels the delta.

show.at: on 'the old patterns were actually cleaner'
show.event: A hardest-cases strip drops in beneath: patterns 1.0000 precision against matcher 0.9929.
Footer sets: the claim is RECALL, 85 holdings recovered, nothing more.

beats.narration_text: Here is one reason why. Some funds write x dot A I, with a dot in the middle. Some write it without. That single dot was hiding eighty-five holdings. And the fund hiding behind it was Fidelity, the largest holder of that company. One character. The biggest holder. Invisible.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w4-scoreboard.png (lower half). Two spellings at display size; the beat lives or dies on the viewer SEEING one character of difference, so the dot is the only terracotta thing on screen until the count lands.

XAI CORP sets directly beneath, aligned character-for-character so the missing dot is unmissable.
The first spelling picks up the tag 'matched by the pattern'; the second picks up 'matched by nothing'.
The counter races to 85 beside the second spelling.
The holder line resolves underneath: Fidelity Mt. Vernon Street Trust.

beats.narration_text: Now the part I did not expect. I had flagged a holding called OpenAir dot com as not one of my companies. I wrote a confident reason. I approved my own judgment. Then I read the actual rows. Five holdings, BlackRock and New York Life, all priced at six eighty-seven point six eight six nine. Which is OpenAI's Series C price, to four decimal places. It was OpenAI the whole time.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w4-reversal.png. The strongest beat in the reel. The five real rows land, then the OpenAI anchor row drops in UNDER them at the identical price — the match is what the viewer should notice a half-second before the narration says it.

A rule draws and the anchor row drops in beneath, terracotta, at the identical price. The two now sit in one column.
The approved stamp is struck through and re-set to OpenAI.

beats.narration_text: My reason had been factually wrong, and my own matcher was throwing those five holdings away. So I withdrew the approval, fixed the matcher, and published the worse number next to the better one. Because a score you measured after fixing what the test caught is not a validation. It is just a score.

shot.visual_intent: The retraction as three committed acts, then the rule that follows. Both scores stay on screen together — publishing only the better one is the failure this beat is about.

props.title: The test overruled me, so I published both scores

props.struckNote: factually wrong — there were five holdings across two period ends
props.rule: A score you measured after fixing what the test caught is not a validation. It is just a score.

beats.narration_text: And there is no threshold that saves you here. A used car marketplace whose name happens to contain open and A I scores exactly the same as three entries that really are SpaceX. And two of those three are the same string, differing only by a trailing space. Point eight zero, all four. No cut-off separates them. So four cases a run go to a person instead.

shot.visual_intent: Rebuild of pantry/w4-tie.png. Four rows at the SAME score — the visual argument is that a horizontal cut-off cannot separate them, so the cut-off is drawn and visibly fails.

beats.narration_text: Week four on one page. Seven companies, a hundred and twenty-eight spellings, three point two million names to hide in. A golden set of three hundred and twenty-two labels, and two systems scored against it. Recall went to a hundred percent, precision did not really improve, and the set caught a label I had already approved. Eight of those three hundred and twenty-two have actually been reviewed by a person. Next week: can a language model beat this? And if it cannot, I say so.

props.artifactTitle: Entity Resolution and the Golden Set — week 4
artifactLines: Seven universe companies file under 128 distinct spellings, hiding inside 3,204,853 distinct issuer names.
Golden set v1.0.0: 322 labelled issuer names covering 7,276 holdings — the same labels judge both systems.
Recall 0.9792 → 1.0000. Precision moved 0.9916 → 0.9959, and on the hardest cases the old patterns were cleaner. The claim is recall.
One missing dot — X.AI CORP vs XAI CORP — hid 85 holdings, and the largest holder of that company files it without.
The set reversed a label I had approved: OpenAir.com = OpenAI at 687.6869. Approval withdrawn, matcher fixed, both scores published. Only 8 of 322 labels are human-reviewed.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. Take a messy list of names out of your own data. Customers, vendors, anything. Label thirty rows by hand with the real entity each one is. Then run whatever matching logic you already have against those labels and measure its recall. Then, and this is the part that matters, go back and find out what your own labelling got wrong. Building the test is the easy half. Being willing to let it overrule you is the whole job.
